item.title: After a deadly wildfire, this school district wasn’t sure if families would return. Eight years later, it’s seeing an influx of students
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

PARADISE, Calif. — Surveying the wreckage in the weeks after the Camp Fire — tens of thousands of people displaced, 85 percent of the town’s buildings destroyed and all but one campus of Paradise Unified School District damaged — it was hard for Jake Timm to imagine when or if the town’s population might recover. It could be 15 or 20 years before enough students returned to fill the schools in the Northern California community, thought Timm, the district’s director of facilities, maintenance and operations.

“I don’t think we knew exactly what we were stepping into,” said Timm. “Especially when we got up here after the fire to assess the damage, when part of the town was still smoldering.”

But after falling precipitously in the years after the 2018 wildfire, California’s deadliest on record, the district’s enrollment began to rebound. Today, it’s up to 1,817 students — still just 53 percent of enrollment pre-fire but enough for the district to speed up the timeline for rebuilding its second elementary school in Paradise to meet demand. This fall the school became the last of the district’s campuses to reopen post-fire, and there are already plans to add new classrooms. An average of just over 80 new students arrive each year.

School districts across the country are dealing with sharp enrollment declines brought about primarily because of falling birthrates, and California’s drop is among the most pronounced. But in Paradise, district officials are seeing an unexpected increase in younger students, as more young families relocate to the area, drawn by its relative affordability and new development.

Still, even as Paradise Unified School District completes the physical rebuilding process, lingering effects on academics show the long tail of post-disaster recovery.

Over a quarter of Paradise Unified’s students are chronically absent, a rate that’s more than 10 percentage points higher than the state average. Graduation rates and state test scores have also suffered.

That aligns with the growing body of research on the impact of wildfires and other disasters on education. In the short term, disasters and extreme weather can lead to increased absences and adverse learning outcomes. Longer term, research has linked experiencing a natural disaster to fewer years of total schooling completed, which in turn can correlate to reduced higher education outcomes and potential lifetime earnings.

And recovering from wildfires and other disasters is becoming an increasingly common challenge for school districts in California and elsewhere, as climate change drives more frequent extreme weather events and more severe disasters. Approximately 25 percent of public schools in the U.S. are located in census tracts designated as very high risk from at least one environmental hazard, including coastal flooding, hurricanes, heat waves and wildfires, according to research from Brown University’s SustainableED initiative. In the coming years, more of them will face difficult questions about if, and how, to rebuild.

Related: When natural disasters strike, these camps give kids a safe place to recover

When Southern California’s Pasadena Unified School District — which faced declining enrollment for over a decade before the January 2025 Eaton Fire destroyed more than 9,000 buildings — weighed consolidating its schools earlier this year, families were outraged. Students who lost their homes in the fire said their still-standing schools offered stability and community; in a local editorial, one parent questioned why the district would consider closing schools so soon after the fire, when rebuilding might draw more families.

And after the 110-year-old King Kamehameha III Elementary School was destroyed in the August 2023 Maui wildfires, the majority of community members wanted the historic campus rebuilt in the same location. But state education officials said the campus couldn’t be rebuilt there because of limited space, flood risk and other factors, and instead chose a different site about a half-mile away and outside of the tsunami inundation zone.

Near Paradise, the tiny Golden Feather Union Elementary School District was also affected by the Camp Fire. The water system at the district’s only school, Concow Elementary, was severely damaged, and overall recovery in the more rural and lower-income community of Concow has been slower than in Paradise. The district relocated students to an elementary campus it had closed back in 2010, where they remain today. The new site is about 8 miles from Concow Elementary and closer to the town of Oroville, where many families relocated.

Only two Paradise Unified schools reopened in their original locations shortly after the fire: Pine Ridge Elementary and Cedarwood Elementary, both located in Magalia, which is just northeast of Paradise. Students from other schools spent the months after the fire scattered across Butte County. The junior high operated out of a hardware store, while the two high schools moved to independent study with drop-in hours at a mall. Paradise Elementary and Ponderosa Elementary, which was also destroyed in the fire, both used classrooms provided by other districts, each 20 miles away from Paradise.

Among the town’s boosters, whether Paradise would rebuild wasn’t really a question. The city started on a long-term recovery plan right after the fire and set goals of making the community more fire-resilient and welcoming to new and returning residents.

“My son was a freshman in high school here in town when this all happened, and he said, ‘I won’t go anywhere but Paradise,’” said Timm. “We’re a very strong-headed community, the ones of us that are left here.”

Two days before the fire, residents had passed a $61 million bond to modernize schools and complete a list of maintenance projects. “We passed the bond, we were all, ‘Woo-hoo,’ and then we’re all evacuating,” said Timm.…

item.title: Writing Is Not a Checkpoint: Teaching Contextual Judgment in the AI Era
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

At the public library desk, questions about writing often arrive as requests for technical help. Patrons drafting personal statements need to decide which details about their experience to include; people completing online forms need to interpret questions before answering them. Helping patrons make writing decisions has been as much a part of my library work as explaining where to click.

I encounter similar questions in online writing courses. Students bring rules such as “never use I,” “always write five paragraphs,” and “never use artificial intelligence.” Some rules are assignment requirements; others are writing conventions students have learned to apply everywhere. Contextual judgment requires understanding what a rule accomplishes and when it applies. Students need opportunities to explain their choices within course requirements and ask for clarification when an expectation is unclear.

Rhetoric and composition scholar Sharon Crowley described required freshman English as a “border checkpoint,” where students had to establish their right to belong in higher education (1991, 160). She argued for ending the universal requirement while retaining the course as an elective (170). I draw on her account of gatekeeping to ask a narrower classroom question: How can instructors teach judgment while assessing compliance with assignment requirements? AI policies establish what is permitted; instruction must help students judge whether a permitted use serves the assignment’s purpose. The following examples illustrate ways to teach contextual judgment through activities and feedback you can adapt to your own courses.

Start with the Rules Students Bring

Nancy Walker, who helped me learn to teach writing, was an English professor and director of freshman English at what was then Southwest Missouri State University. In her 1987 statement, “Thoughts About Teaching,” she described how students could move from rigid right-or-wrong thinking to the belief that every judgment was a matter of personal preference. She called for “contextual deciding,” in which students evaluate ideas in context, commit to a choice, and remain willing to reconsider it (2).

A writing rules inventory offers one way to practice contextual deciding. Early in the course, ask students to list three rules they have learned. Have them choose one and explain where they learned it, what purpose it might serve, and when it might be useful. Follow the inventory with examples that test the rule’s limits.

To test “never use I,” compare two sentences. “I interviewed three residents” identifies who gathered the evidence. If a writer has verified a survey’s respondent count, adding “I believe” to “The survey had 40 respondents” makes the count sound uncertain. In this example, the qualification is unnecessary; the first-person pronoun is not the problem. Ask students to explain the difference, revise the rule, and test it on a sentence from a draft. Discuss how the revised rule accounts for the writer’s purpose.

Make Transfer Explicit

Walker urged teachers to plan activities that make discovery possible (1987, 1–2). Students who have already written a research paper may need help identifying what a new research task asks them to do differently.

The Elon Statement on Writing Transfer emphasizes reflection on how writers adapt prior learning to new tasks (Center for Engaged Learning 2015). For a memo recommending a course of action to a busy supervisor, ask students to write a brief transfer note before they draft the memo. Which practices from an earlier research essay can they reuse? What will they need to change for this reader and purpose?

Ask students to identify one adjustment, such as placing a recommendation before its supporting explanation. After students draft the memo, have them revisit the note and explain how a specific passage addresses the supervisor’s needs. Compare the passage with the explanation and give feedback on any needed revision. Students can consult the note when deciding whether the same strategy fits a later assignment.

Use the Problem as Material

Walker described a student who was stuck writing about his father. She helped him notice that his draft expressed affection as well as criticism (1987, 3–4). When students hesitate over an AI revision, ask them to compare the original and suggested wording and explain how the change affects the claim. The Association for Writing Across the Curriculum recommends reflection on whether and how AI serves a writing task (AWAC Working Group on AI in WAC 2025).

Explain permitted uses of AI before students begin an assignment. A process note does not authorize prohibited assistance. After major assignments in my online writing courses, I ask for an AI Use Note or process note that acknowledges assistance and examines the writer’s decisions:

- What tools or other assistance did you use, and for which parts of the assignment?

- Which suggestions did you accept, change, or reject, and why?

- How did you check the claims and sources you used?

- What alternatives did you consider for one writing decision, and why did you choose your approach?

Students who worked without AI can describe research and revision decisions. For students who used AI, the note should address how they evaluated AI suggestions and whether their use met the assignment’s rules. Instructors can collect the note with a draft and give feedback students can use during revision.

If students cite a source without reading it, ask them to read it and check whether it supports the claim. Have students correct any unsupported claim or inaccurate citation. Read the note alongside the draft to discuss whether the explanation matches the writing. A plausible explanation alone does not establish authorship or compliance.…

item.title: End With the Heart: Sustaining Compassionate Connections
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

As the semester begins to come to a close, something shifts in the room. The energy changes. There is a quiet mixture of fatigue, anticipation, pressure, and, at times, disconnection. Students are holding many things at once. Deadlines, uncertainty, personal responsibilities, and hopes for what comes next. As faculty, we are often holding just as much.

If we begin our courses with the heart, then we are called to end them the same way.

The final weeks of a course are not simply about finishing content or assigning final grades. They are about how we accompany our students through a meaningful transition. They are about how we hold the learning, the relationships, and the lived experiences that have unfolded over time. Ending with the heart invites us to remain present, to stay relational, and to approach closure with the same compassion that grounded the beginning. This relational approach to teaching echoes hooks’ (1994) vision of education as a practice rooted in connection, presence, and shared humanity.

Returning to Compassion in the Closing Weeks

Compassion, as Gilbert (2009) reminds us, involves an attunement to suffering with a commitment to respond to it. Neff (2003, 2023) expands this understanding by emphasizing self-compassion as the practice of relating to ourselves with kindness, recognizing our shared humanity, and remaining mindfully present with our experiences. Germer (2009) further describes compassion as a moment-to-moment process of turning toward difficulty with care rather than avoidance, allowing us to meet challenges with warmth and understanding.

In the final weeks of a course, this attunement becomes especially important. Students may not always name what they are carrying, but we can often feel it. Increased anxiety. Self-doubt. Exhaustion. A sense of urgency. A feeling of being overwhelmed and overextended.

Ending with the heart means softening into self-kindness, remembering our shared humanity, and staying present with what is, rather than what we wish had been. It is not about removing the challenge but about holding it with care.

Holding the Home Stretch with Intention

The final weeks benefit from clarity and steadiness. When expectations are clearly communicated and thoughtfully organized, students can exhale, even if just a little. A simple roadmap of what remains, paired with reassurance, can reduce uncertainty and support focus.

At the same time, compassion invites us to ask ourselves: What truly matters now? What are the essential learning experiences we want students to carry with them?

When we align our expectations with what is meaningful rather than excessive, we create space for deeper engagement rather than overwhelm. This is not about lowering standards. It is about teaching with intention and discernment.

Staying Connected as Energy Shifts

It is natural for engagement to change as the semester winds down. Students may feel pulled in many directions. Rather than interpreting this as disengagement, we can approach it with curiosity and care.

Inviting students to reflect on their learning can gently reawaken connection. What has stayed with you? What challenged you? Where have you grown?

One simple practice I often use is inviting students into a brief “glow and grow” reflection—naming something they are proud of and something they are continuing to develop. This creates space for both celebration and self-compassion, allowing students to hold their learning with balance and care.

These moments do not need to be complex. Sometimes a brief reflection, a shared conversation, or a pause to acknowledge the collective experience of the semester can bring the room back together.

Naming what is present matters. When we say, “This is a full time for many of us,” we remind students that they are not alone. That sense of shared humanity can be grounding in ways that are often understated but deeply felt.

Tending to Stress with Compassion

The end of the semester can be one of the most stressful periods for students and faculty alike. Bringing small moments of care into our classrooms can make a meaningful difference.

This might look like a brief pause for a breath. A moment to check in. A gentle reminder that it is okay to feel overwhelmed. These practices do not take away from learning. They support it.

Encouraging self-compassion during this time can help students shift how they relate to their own struggles. Rather than moving into cycles of self-criticism, they can begin to meet themselves with kindness and understanding. Research suggests that self-compassion supports emotional resilience and reduces distress (Neff, 2003).

When we model this ourselves, even in small ways, we offer students permission to do the same.

Creating Meaningful Last-Day Experiences

The final class session holds a particular kind of significance. It is a moment of closure, but also of integration.

Rather than filling this time with only final logistics, we can create space for reflection. Inviting students to share what they are taking with them, what mattered, or what they are proud of can be deeply grounding.

There is something powerful about being witnessed at the end of a journey.

Expressions of gratitude can also be meaningful. When we take a moment to acknowledge our students, not only for what they have done but for who they have been in the space, it reinforces their sense of belonging and worth.

Extending Connection Beyond the Final Class

Ending with the heart does not have to stop when the final class session ends.

One practice I have found deeply meaningful is sending a follow-up email to students after the course concludes. In this message, I gently recap our shared journey. I reflect on moments of growth I witnessed, themes that emerged, and the ways students showed up for one another and for themselves.

This is not an evaluation. It is a continuation of the relational space we built together.…
